Subject: Endodontics
Question: Which is the best storage medium for avulsed tooth at the scene of injury among the following:
Explanation:
[Clinical and Practical Implications of Storage Media used for Tooth Avulsion. Int J Clin Pediatr Dent. 2017 Apr-Jun; 10(2): 158-165.]
Based on the literature, solutions designed specifically for storage and culture purposes (HBSS, VIASPAN) are the best for storing avulsed tooth. But if they are not available, regular pasteurized whole milk is the most frequently recommended and with the best prognosis among other solutions that are likely to be available at the scene of an accident, such as water, saline or saliva. Its advantages include its high availability, ready accessibility, physiologically compatible pH and osmolality (fluid pressure) with the root-surface adhered PDL cells, presence of nutrients and growth factors.

Various Storage media:
• Cell and tissue culture solutions like Hank's Balanced Salt Solution (HBSS)
• Medical/hospital products developed specifically for organ storage purposes, such as Viaspan
• Culture media, like Minimum Essential Medium (MEM)
• Saline
• Natural products like water, saliva, bovine milk and its variations, propolis, green tea, Morus rubra (red mulberry), egg white and coconut water
• Rehydrating solutions, like Gatorade and Ricetral
• Contact lens solutions

Contact lens solutions are essentially saline solutions. Studies showed that the solutions for keeping contact lenses were worse than saline solution, milk, and HBSS. The presence of preservatives in its formula was harmful to the cells of the PDL and therefore, they are not recommended.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: PAD wavelength for sterilization of root canal?
Explanation:
[Ingle 6th ed 970]
Photoactivated disinfection (PAD) also called as Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) involves the use of dyes or photosensitizers (tolonium chloride) that are introduced into the root canal system and activated by laser light with a wavelength corresponding to the absorption maximum of the dye.
• These wavelengths are typically within the visible (from 635 to 675 nm) and near-infrared (810 nm) spectrum.
• Besides the presence of a specific light source in the target area, this application also requires the presence of sufficient oxygen in the tissue.
• When all these conditions are satisfied, the exposure of the dye to the light drives a photochemical reaction producing free radicals and singlet oxygen that finally generate the bactericidal effect.

Question: Addition of copper in NiTi alloy results in all except?
Option A: better tarnish and corrosion resistance of the alloy
Option B: increases transition temperature range of the alloy
Option C: does not affect so much its superplastic property
Option D: exerts a high loading and low unloading force
Explanation:
[Mechanical properties of NiTi and CuNiTi wires used in orthodontic treatment. Dental Press J Orthod. 2014 Jan-Feb; 19(1): 69-76]
Copper is one of the third element that has been added to nickel-titanium, resulting in a copper-nickel-titanium alloy with many potential clinical advantages in orthodontics. Manufacturing companies claim that the addition of copper would allow the orthodontist to more easily engage larger arch wires. This is because the copper lowers the loading stress while still providing relatively high unloading stress resulting in more effective orthodontic tooth movement of teeth. This is known as having a lower stress hysteresis.

Advantages of adding copper to Ni-Ti:
• Stabilizes the superelasticity characteristics against cyclic deformation.
• reduces the ageing effect of Ni-Ti.
• Improved corrosion resistance.
• Better defined transition temperatures, which not only ensures the generation of more homogeneous loadings from arch to arch and from end to end, but also increases the effectiveness of tooth movement.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Deeper invasion of root dentin by resorbing tissues that extend into the coronal third of the root comes under which class of Heithersay’s classification
Explanation:
[Ingle 5th ed 141]
Invasive cervical resorption:
• Extracanal invasive resorption, also termed invasive cervical resorption, is given by Heithersay.
• In this the pulp remains unaffected until late in the process owing to an apparently thin and resorption-resistant layer of dentin and predentin. This separates the pulp from the ingrowing tissue that is initially fibrovascular in character but becomes a fibro-osseous type of tissue.
• If exposed to the oral cavity, the pulp will be invaded by microorganisms. Although pulp vitality can be maintained if there is early diagnosis and treatment of this type of resorption, more extensive lesions require nonsurgical root canal therapy and resorption treatment if the tooth is to be retained.

Heithersay's Classification (Invasive Cervical Resorption):
Class 1: Small, invasive resorptive lesion near the cervical area with shallow penetration into the dentin.
Class II: Well defined, invasive resorptive lesion that has penetrated close to the coronal pulp but with little or no extension into the radicular dentin.
Class III: Deeper invasion of root dentin by resorbing tissues that extend into the coronal third of the root.
Class IV: Large, invasive resorptive process that extend beyond the coronal third of the root.

Question: Classification of Kim’s microsurgical endodontic case having a large periapical lesion approaching coronally with no pocket and no mobility:
Explanation:
[Microsurgery in Endodontics by Syngcuk Kim 1st ed 21] Syngcuk Kim and Kratchman classified Endodontic Microsurgical Cases periradicular lesions into categories A-F. Class A: Represents the absence of a periapical lesion, no mobility, and normal pocket depth, but unresolved symptoms after nonsurgical approaches have been exhausted. Clinical symptoms are the only reason for the surgery. Class B: Represents the presence of a small periapical lesion together with clinical symptoms. The tooth has normal periodontal probing depth and no mobility. The teeth in this class are ideal candidates for microsurgery. Class C: Teeth have a large periapical lesion progressing coronally, but without periodontal pocket and mobility. Class D: Features are clinically similar to those in Class C, but have deep periodontal pockets. Class E: Teeth have a deep periapical lesion with an endodontic-periodontal communication to the apex but no obvious fracture. Class F: Represents a tooth with an apical lesion and complete denudement of the buccal plate but no mobility. Lesion types A, B, and C represent lesions of endodontic origin and are ranked according to increasing size of periradicular radiolucency. Lesion types D, E, and F represent lesions of combined endodontic-periodontal origin and are ranked according to the magnitude of periradicular breakdown. Classes A, B, and C present no significant treatment problems, and the conditions do not adversely affect treatment outcomes. Classes D, E, and F present serious difficulties.

Question: Removal of GP with rotary instrument is done at a speed of:
Explanation:
[Cohen 11th ed 350]
Using rotary systems to remove gutta-percha in the canals has been advocated due to enhanced efficiency and effectiveness in removing gutta-percha from treated root canals. Several types of mechanical rotary systems are available for gutta-percha removal, including the ProFile, the Canal Finder, and dedicated gutta-percha removal instruments, such as the GPX, the Quantec SC, the ProTaper Universal retreatment files, and the Mtwo R. These engine-driven instruments mechanically chop-up the gutta-percha and frictionally thermoplasticizing the root filling mass via frictional heat to aid in removal.

The optimum rotary speed is 1500 rpm for GP removal with various rotary systems. Earlier the speed range was from 350-700 rpm, where instrument fractures were more frequent. Studies demonstrated that when the instrument rotary speed was increased from 350 to 1500 rpm, there was less frequency of fracture.

Question: Not a cannula in ultrafil 3D:
Explanation:
[Cohen 11th ed 310]
• Ultrafil 3D is a thermoplastic gutta-percha injection technique involving gutta-percha cannulas, a heating unit, and an injection syringe.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Which of the following does not dissolve MTA
Explanation:
[Effect of various chemicals as solvents on the dissolution of set white mineral trioxide aggregate: an in vitro study. J Endod. 2010 Jan;36(1):135-8]
Because MTA is alkaline in nature, it might interact with acids or chemicals and could disintegrate. Few studies have been done to evaluate the effect of chemicals on MTA.

Nandini et al tested the effect of carbonic acid, 2% chlorhexidine gluconate, 17% EDTA and saline on set white MTA (WMTA) on 1 day and 21 days after setting. They concluded that:
• Carbonic acid can be effectively used as an adjunct to dissolve set WMTA even after 21 days, whereas 2% chlorhexidine gluconate showed significant surface dissolution only within 24 hours of WMTA placement. Thus, usage of chlorhexidine gluconate as a root canal irrigant in which WMTA is used during endodontic procedure should be avoided for 24 hours.
• Solutions with EDTA have no effect on surface hardness of WMTA.
• Another study which compared dissolution of a mineral trioxide aggregate sealer in endodontic solvents compared to conventional sealers concluded that chloroform was effective in dissolving MTA based root canal sealers. [Dissolution of a mineral trioxide aggregate sealer in endodontic solvents compared to conventional sealers. Braz Oral Res.2016;30.]

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Apexum is used for?
Option D: Minimally invasive method for the debridement of periradicular tissue
Explanation:
[Cohen 10th ed 241]
In nonsurgical endodontic procedures, the healing of apical periodontitis is achieved by treatment provided within the root canal system. The new Apexum procedure is based on advancing the debridement one step further by minimally invasive removal of the inflamed periapical tissues through root canal access, thereby enhancing the healing kinetics of periapical lesions.

The Apexum procedure uses 2 sequential rotary devices designed to extend beyond the apex and to mince periapical tissues on rotation in a low-speed hand piece, followed by washing out the minced tissue. The Apexum kit consists of two devices, the Apexum NiTi Ablator and Apexum PGA Ablator, designed to be used sequentially.

1) Apexum NiTi Ablator consists of a specially pre shaped Nitinol wire. One end is bent and is designed to enter the periapical tissues through the root canal and apical foramen, whereas the other end has a latch-type connector to allow its operation by a low-speed contra-angle handpiece. The bent part is initially concealed in a straight superelastic Nitinol tube that serves as a sheath allowing its introduction up to the apical foramen. When pushed, the wire emerges from its sheath and through the apical foramen and resumes its pre shaped form. The special retrograde design of the bent part allows it to rotate in the periapical soft tissues at 200 to 250 rpm and coarsely grind them while being deflected from the surrounding bone. The Nitinol sheath is used first to allow the introduction of the pre bent Nitinol wire to the apical foramen and second to allow unobstructed rotation of the wire in the root canal without twisting of the wire.

2) The second device is the Apexum PGA Ablator, built from a Nitinol shaft, equipped on one end with a latch-type connector to allow its operation by a low-speed contra-angle handpiece. At the other end, a bioabsorbable filament is attached, which is designed to enter the peri-apical bony crypt and rotate at 5,000 to 7,000 rpm, turning the tissue that was initially minced with the NiTi Ablator into a thin suspension that may be flushed through the root canal.

Apexum procedure:
• A #20 K-file is passed through the apical foramen and beyond the apex to verify patency. It is followed by a rotary #30 file that is passed 1 mm beyond the apical foramen, creating a passage with a 330 μm diameter.
• The Apexum NiTi Ablator is then inserted, while encased in its sheath, to the working length as established at the cleaning and shaping stage.
• The sheath is stabilized to the occlusal surface of the tooth using glass-ionomer cement. The Nitinol filament is then pushed manually through the enlarged apical foramen and into the periapical tissues.
• The NiTi Ablator is then rotated in the periapical tissues for 30 seconds at 200 to 250 rpm to initially mince the tissue. The stabilizing glass-ionomer cement is then removed, and the NiTi Ablator withdrawn from the root canal with its sheath. Root canal is then rinsed with sterile saline, and the Apexum PGA Ablator is manually inserted through the root canal and into the periapical tissues. It is then connected to a low-speed contra-angle hand piece and rotated for 30 seconds at 5,000 to 7,000 rpm to turn the minced tissues into a thin suspension. Next, it is withdrawn from the root canal. The tissue suspension is now washed out with sterile saline solution.

Question: Not a component of endoflass ?
Explanation:
[Pediatric dentistry by Nikhil Marwah 4th ed 678]
Endoflas is a resorbable paste produced in South America which contains components similar to that of Vitapex, Zinc oxide, and Eugenol.

Endoflas Composition:
• This paste is obtained by mixing a powder containing tri-iodomethane and iodine dibutylorthocresol (40.6%), Zinc oxide (56.5%), Calcium hydroxide (1.07%) and Barium sulfate (1.63%).
• The rationale behind incorporating three materials Zinc oxide Eugenol, Calcium hydroxide, and Iodoform into Endoflas was probably to compensate the disadvantage of one individual material with the advantages of the other.
• Endoflas paste has the advantage of having the resorption limited to the excess material, which has been extruded. Resorption of the material does not occur within the canal. Thus, the material is neither resistant to resorption nor does it result in the hollow tube effect.
• The manufacturers of endoflas paste claims that it has a broad spectrum of antibacterial efficacy.
• The material is hydrophilic and can be used in mildly humid canals. It has the ability to disinfect dentinal tubules and hard-to-reach accessory canals that cannot be disinfected or cleansed mechanically. In addition, the components of the material can be removed by phagocytosis making it resorbable.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Compressive strength of biodentine after 30 days ?
Explanation:
[Comparison of physical and mechanical properties of mineral trioxide aggregate and Biodentine. Indian J Dent Res 2014;25:692-7]
Biodentine is a tricalcium silicate-based cement. The material is claimed to possess better physical and biological properties compared to other tricalcium silicate cements such as MTA and Bioaggregate.
• It is a premixed and liquid system where the powder is composed of tricalcium silicate (main component), calcium carbonate (filler material), zirconium oxide (radiopacifier), dicalcium silicate (traces), calcium oxide (traces), iron oxide (traces) and the liquid is an aqueous solution of a hydrosoluble polymer (water reducing agent) with calcium chloride (decreases setting time).
• Biodentine has a wide range of applications including endodontic repair (root perforations, apexification, resorptive lesions, and retrograde filling material in endodontic surgery) and pulp capping and can be used as a dentine replacement material in restorative dentistry. The material is actually formulated using the MTA-based cement technology and the improvement of some properties of these types of cements, such as physical qualities and handling.
• Setting time: The working time of Biodentine is up to 6 minutes with a final set at around 9-12 minutes. This represents a great improvement compared to MTA, which set in more than 2 hours.
• Compressive strength: A specific feature of Biodentine is its capacity to continue improving with time in terms of strength over several days until reaching 300 MPa after one month. This value becomes quite stable and is in the range of the compressive strength of natural dentine (297 MPa). Grech et al. studied that Biodentine showed highest compressive strength as compared to other tested materials due to its low water: powder ratio. The compressive strength of MTA-Angelus was 41 MPa at 24 hour that increased to 76.8 MPa at 28 days.
• Vickers hardness: Biodentine exhibits sufficient hardness to be used as dental material. After 2 hours, the hardness of biodentine is 51 VHN and reaches 69 VHN after 1 month.

Question: Tunnel defects are seen in?
Option B: Proximal cavity preparation from occlusal side
Explanation:
[Ingle 5th ed 870]
• Dentin bridge formation has been considered to be the sign of success in response to direct pulp capping procedures.
• Calcium Hydroxide has no inherent adhesive qualities and provides a poor seal. The appearance of so-called tunnel defects in reparative dentin formed underneath calcium hydroxide pulp caps has been reported.
• A tunnel defect has been described as a patency from the site of the exposure through the reparative dentin to the pulp, sometimes with fibroblasts and capillaries present within the defect.
• Cox and Subay found that 89% of bridges formed in response to calcium hydroxide direct pulp caps demonstrated tunnel defects, which allowed access of microleakage products beneath the restoration into the pulp. They found recurrent pulp inflammation beneath 41% of all bridges formed in the sample.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: The needle used in irrigation which is the most important factor:
Option C: Final size of root canal preparation
Explanation:
[Ingle 5th ed 502]
The factors affecting the efficacy of needle irrigation include:
• The diameter of the irrigating needle,
• Needle design,
• Depth of the irrigating needle, and
• The final size of the root canal preparation.

Some important points:
• Narrower gauge needles (27 or 30 gauge) are more effective than larger gauge needles in removing debris from curved canals. Needles with gauges of 27 and 30 present external diameter of 0.4 and 0.3 mm, respectively.
• The use of a close-ended single side vented needle is considered to be the safest needle design for irrigation.
• Positioning the needle as close to the working length (WL) as possible to improve debridement and irrigant replacement is advocated.
• Wedging a needle in a canal is dangerous and can cause serious sequelae.
• Canal size and shape are crucial to the penetration of the irrigant. The apical 5 mm are not flushed until they have been enlarged to size 30 and more often to size 40 file.

Question: Heithersay’s classification of large invasive resorptive process that extend till middle third of root.
Explanation:
[Ingle 5th ed 141]
Heithersay's Classification (Invasive Cervical Resorption):
Class 1: Small, invasive resorptive lesion near the cervical area with shallow penetration into the dentin.
Class II: Well defined, invasive resorptive lesion that has penetrated close to the coronal pulp but with little or no extension into the radicular dentin.
Class III: Deeper invasion of root dentin by resorbing tissues that extend into the coronal third of the root.
Class IV: Large, invasive resorptive process that extend beyond the coronal third of the root.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: True statement regarding leaving the tooth open during RCT in apical abscess
Option B: Should not be left open in any case
Option C: Patient is made to sit for some time to allow drainage and then closed
Option D: Should be left open if swelling is present
Explanation:
[Check Explanation Below]
Earlier whenever swelling and persistent drainage was present, the root canals were left open in between the visits. But current research has shown that the access opening in the tooth must be sealed with an effective interappointment filling to prevent microbial contamination by microleakage from the oral cavity.

Based on the most current evidence-based literature published in peer-reviewed journals, canals should NOT be left “open to drain”- Stephen Cohen

One study showed that the root canals that had been unsealed at some point during the treatment, had a higher frequency of enteric bacteria than in canals with an adequate seal between the appointments.

Leaving a tooth open for drainage is contraindicated as it can cause contamination from the oral cavity and lead to flare ups. Drainage should be allowed under the rubber dam, if drainage is persistent, the patient should be made to sit for some time and the tooth closed immediately after the treatment to prevent secondary infections.

Question: Pulpitis pain is
Option A: Dull throbbing mediated by A beta
Option B: Fast and sharp piercing mediated by A delta
Option C: Dull throbbing myelinated mediated by C fibers
Option D: Dull throbbing unmyelinated mediated by C fibers
Explanation:
[Check 2017-18 recent paper in endodontics]
Pain in pulpitis is dull throbbing type mediated by unmyelinated C fibers of the pulp. Dental hypersensitivity is characterized by sharp pain mediated by myelinated A delta fibers.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: True about phoenix abscess ?
Explanation:
[Ingle 5th ed 182]
The extent of the chronic periapical lesion (asymptomatic apical lesion) depends on the potency of the irritants within the root canal system and the activity level of defensive factors in this region. If a balance between these forces is maintained, the lesion continues in an asymptomatic manner indefinitely.

On the other hand, if the causative factors overcome the defensive elements, a symptomatic periradicular lesion may be superimposed on the asymptomatic one. This is one example of the so-called Phoenix abscess.

Question: False positive result is shown by
Explanation:
[Grossman 12th ed 68] False positive results: • A false positive response is where a non-vital tooth appears to respond positively to testing. • Anxious or young patients who may report a premature response because they are anticipating an unpleasant sensation. • Necrotic breakdown products in one part of a root canal system can conduct electric currents to viable nerve tissue in adjacent areas. • Contact with metal restorations may also result in conduction of the current to the periodontium. • Inadequately dried teeth. False negative results: • A false negative result means that a vital tooth has not responded positively to testing. • Incomplete root development, which have a higher threshold to testing, and require a stronger stimulation than normal to elicit a response (cold testing is more reliable here). • Traumatized teeth may not respond to thermal or EPT due to nerve rupture. • Orthodontic tooth movement. • Patients with psychotic disorders. • Patients under sedative drugs.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: To prevent error while doing access opening of maxillary 1st premolar one should be aware of
Explanation:
[Cohen 8th ed 192]
The cervical width of maxillary 1st premolar is narrower mesiodistally, the clinician must be cautious to avoid mesiodistal perforation. There is also a concavity on mesial side, which makes the area below pulp chamber laterally thin. So the clinician must take care not to over extend the preparation in that direction as it may lead to perforation.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: Occlusal reduction after RCT should be done in
Option A: Non vital tooth with TOP (tender on percussion) negative
Option C: Vital tooth or non-vital with periapical pathology
Explanation:
[Endodontics E-Book by Kishor Gulabivala 4th ed 270]
Some clinicians recommend occlusal reduction, but such an approach should only be adopted following a proper occlusal assessment. The tooth will not stay out of contact for long because of continued eruption. Occlusal reduction works when there had been previous presence of percussion sensitivity, in vital cases and in the absence of a periapical radiolucency. However, research do not recommend it as a routine procedure.

After instrumentation of vital teeth with a history of pain and percussion sensitivity, occlusal reduction has been shown to be important in preventing post treatment pain. - Cohen 8th ed 81

Rosenberg et al reported in his study, occlusal reduction should prevent postoperative pain in those patients whose teeth initially exhibit pulp vitality, percussion sensitivity, preoperative pain, and/or the absence of periradicular radiolucency.

Subject: Endodontics
Question: When radicular cyst is connected to apical foramen it is termed as
Explanation:
[Cohen 10th ed 326]
• There are two types of periapical cysts: the periapical true cyst and the periapical pocket cyst.
• True cysts have a contained cavity or lumen within a continuous epithelial lining and are therefore isolated from the tooth, whereas with pocket cysts, the lumen is open to the root canal of the affected tooth.
• True cysts, due to their self-sustaining nature, probably do not heal following nonsurgical endodontic therapy and usually require surgical enucleation.
